description.narrative:
1.1 Riverine communities are one of the most vulnerable populations to climate change. Building the adaptive capacity of these communities will also factor in economic resilience. Participation in economic activities and trade would not only ensure food security but also build economic resilience. Through its interventions in T23R CUTS will contribute to the economic resilience of the riverine communities in three river basins namely, Ganges (Mahakali and Lower Ganges), Brahmaputra and Meghna. 1.2 The geographic outreach CUTS in the Brahmaputra basin will include Assam (Dhubri and Kokrajhar); Meghalaya (Garo hills); Sikkim and West Bengal covering thesub-basin of Teesta and South Salmara-Mankachar covering the sub-basin Jinjiram. 1.3 Both Dhubri and South Salmara-Mankachar districts fall in lower Assam and are located along the bank of the Brahmaputra River. They have numerous chars (islands formed in the middle of a river) and hence, waterways are a major means of transportation in these districts. These locations also have a blended culture of various racial groups including locals and migrants. The district is socioeconomically backward with 41.5 per cent poverty (Statistical Handbook of Assam, 2016). The riverine communities face floods every year and are also susceptible to erosion. The economy is primarily agrarian and the society is patriarchal. Women are mostly engaged in household chores and livestock and poultry rearing. 1.4 In the Meghna basin, CUTS will intervene in Janitia Hills, East Khasi Hills and South Garo Hills of Meghalaya as well as the Barak Valley of Assam. The indigenous communities in Meghalaya have matrilineal societies wherein women are actively involved in economic activities like farming, trade and tourism. 1.5 In the Mahakali basin, CUTS will cover Pittoragarh, and Champawat districtsof Uttarakhand and Pilibhit and Lekhimpur Kheri in Uttar Pradesh to undertake the study on green value chain and undertake the need assessment on climate resilient agricultural practices.Women are mostly involved in agrarian activities and collecting forest produce including medicinal plants. There is a significant number of female head households due to male outmigration.
2. Historical background, Impact, outcomes up to now and theirlimits (brief about RRR previous phase work- if applicable). 2.1 In the previous phase of RRR, CUTS explored the potential of short-haul cross-border trade through select inland waterways stretches between India and Bangladesh. Our research work on the waterway stretch Sonamura-Daudkandi contributed to the declaration of that stretch as a Protocol Route between India and Bangladesh. Along with Oxfam India, Oxfam Bangladesh, NERSWN and GUK, we generated evidence regarding the potential benefits of trade via the inland waterway between Dhubri (Assam) and Chilmari (Bangladesh) falling under the India BangladeshProtocol Route-1. 2.2 The multi-stakeholder dialogues and traders’ meetings organised by CUTS, brought together the private sector,academia and theimplementing agencies into one platform to build consensus on inclusive cross-border trade practices through waterways. Our advocacy has contributed to the enhanced trade happening through waterways using low-draft vessels, particularly between Dhubri andChilmari and also to the declaration of the new Protocol Route Sonamura-Daudkandi. 2.3 However, the movement of agriculturalcommodities through these waterways has not materialized yet owing to limited awareness among stakeholders, and some regulatoryand infrastructural challenges. Similarly, other potential waterways can benefit the local marginalised communities living in the international border areas of India and Bangladesh. Such waterways need to be identified and explored for economic benefits andthe policymakers and other beneficiary stakeholders need to be apprised of these benefits for favourable policy actions.
3. Existing capacities (Oxfam and partners)  Established contacts/networks in project areas with local communities/community-based organisations  Constant engagement with implementing agencies in government departments as well as private sector  Technical expertise in research-based advocacy  Strategic joint interventions at basin level with basin-wise partners
4. Projectcontext: What is the current situation Summary of the action plan: Objectives, main components, key stakeholders, and some key figures The overall aim of CUTS interventions is to contribute in building economic resilience of the riverine communitiesintheGBM basins by creating an enabling environment for sub-regional/regional cooperation. As such the proposed interventions will lead to the following outcomes: Outcome 1: Strengthened climate-resilient livelihoods of communities living in the transboundary GBM river basins Outcome 2: Improved and inclusive management of transboundary river ecosystems across the GBM river basins Outcome 3: Strengthened leadership of civil society, especially women, Indigenous People, and youth to influence governmentand private sector on water governance across and between the transboundary GBM basins
Outcome 4: Strengthened cooperation, collaboration and accountability across and between the transboundary GBM river basins
5. Stakeholders and potentialrole intheRRR Phase-2: Including stakeholders mapping and power analysis The key stakeholdersinclude: Government Departments: Inland Waterways Authority of India, Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority, Ministry of Water Resources, Ministry of JalSakti, Forest Department, Customs Department Private sector: traders, shipping companies, vessel owners,country boat owners association, fish processors, fisherfolks association, Community: youth, women, fisherfolks, agro producers, consumers, artisans, homestayowners 6. External context: Challenges and opportunities 6.1 The indigenous communities in the Khasi and Garo Hills of Meghalaya are quite interested in trade with Bangladesh as these hills are rich in natural resources. However, the poorroad infrastructure and non-functional customs stations in those areas make trade an expensive affair because of high logistics costs. Waterways could be an easy alternative to road transport if supported by necessary infrastructure, regulations and facilities. For this, the stakeholders (in both countries) need to be consulted, the potential benefits of using waterways should be gauged and the competent agencies in both countries should agree upon operationalizing it. The opportunity lies in the interest ofindigenouscommunities and traders and the challenge is to get approval from both the governments and its operationalization. 6.2 Concerning Teesta, Bangladesh has been demanding a water-sharing agreement with India as the lean season flow is very low and affectsmillions of farmers downstream and their livelihoods. It is to be noted that summer irrigated rice is quite popular in Bangladesh and eastern India which has elevated the water demand. To develop a sustainable solution to the crisis a proper understanding ofthe Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem nexus is essential and it is pertinent to generate such evidence from India and Bangladesh. The challenge is that Teesta water is a politically sensitive issue in both countries and hence the ‘transboundary’ elementof the study is to be discussed prudently with all stakeholders.
6.3 Furthermore, parts of North Bengal and Sikkim falling in the Teesta basin are popular destinations that attract a significant number of domestic and international touristsevery year.Homestaysrun/owned/managed by women are getting increasingly popular, particularly in offbeat locations. They are the prime source of income for these women and contribute to the financial stability of their families and communities. However, theincreased touristinflux has started impacting the environment adversely. Hence CUTS propose conducting a scoping study to understand the existing challenges in the tourism sector and prepare a manual on sustainable tourism which will be used for capacity building inthe subsequent years.
6.4 The communities in the Mahakali basin are susceptible to floods almost every year. The riverine communities are mostly dependent on agriculture as their primary source of income. CUTS will be undertaking a need assessment of climate-resilient agricultural practices in the basin that will look into the manifestations of climate change and how it is impacting the livelihood and propose suggestions for interventions that can be undertaken in the subsequent years.
6.5 Similarly, thewomen folks in the Indo-Nepal border in the Mahakali basin are involved in non-timber forest produce collection. A proper assessment of the value chain of these products has not been done yet. Such an analysis would highlight the existing gaps, andwomen’srole in the value chain and also bring in the prospects of a cross-border value chain.
6.6 The external challenges that could impact the interventions planned are the political unrest at local/national levels and the upcomingelections.
7. Internalcontext: Strengths we can rely on and weaknesses we should address 7.1 Strengths: Expertise of regional partners, institutions created by local partners, brand name of TROSA in the context of transboundary water governance, established contacts/networks. 7.2 Weakness: Partners working in silos, linking every activity to the upstream-downstream/ transboundary levels- forthis, local partners with similar capacities are essential both in the upstream and the downstream.

participating-org.narrative: CUTS Geneva, is a non-profit NGO that catalyses the pro-trade, pro-equity voices of the Global South in international trade and development debates in Geneva. Through its main three pillars, vis-à-vis, international trade and development, regulations, and governance, CUTS has a robust history of working in areas such as regional integration, agriculture, environment, competition, investment and consumer protection, sustainability, gender, among others. Since its establishment in 2008, CUTS Geneva has provided research-based advocacy and capacity building support through projects in the Global South - where it has real grassroot level networks and partners. CUTS today is well positioned as the prime interlocutor of developing countries and international organisations in Geneva. In Geneva, CUTS collaborates closely with developing country trade experts and negotiators, backing them with technical knowledge and updates on the situation on the ground. CUTS is also the trusted technical cooperation and knowledge partner of international organizations such as the WTO and UNCTAD, where it has consultative status. CUTS Geneva, along with its sister CUTS organizations in India,Kenya, Zambia, Vietnam, USA and Ghana have made footprints in the realm of economicgovernance across the developing world. Our activities stretch from Asia to Africa, South America and beyond.
